text: In Horseshoe Canyon, in southern Utah, a long sandstone wall called the Great Gallery is covered with painted figures. Some stand taller than a grown man, with wide shoulders and hollow eyes, and many have no legs. Nobody knows for certain who painted them.
more: Some of the figures seem to float. You reach them by walking a long way down a sandy canyon.

text: High on a cliff in Capitol Reef National Park, a small stone storehouse still stands. The Fremont people built little granaries like it to keep corn and seeds dry and safe from mice. The rock above works as a roof.
more: Granaries like this are still found tucked into ledges across southern and eastern Utah, some with their doors in place.

text: The word Utah comes from the Ute people. The Ute lived in the mountains and valleys of this land and moved with the seasons, hunting, fishing and gathering. Spanish travelers wrote their name as Yuta, and English speakers later turned it into Utah.
more: The Ute call themselves Nuche, which means the People.

text: The Goshute lived in the dry western desert near the Great Salt Lake, where water is scarce. They knew where every spring was. They gathered pine nuts, seeds and roots, and they hunted rabbits and birds.
more: In autumn, families gathered to harvest pine nuts from the piñon pines, then stored them for winter.

text: In the red-rock country of southeastern Utah live the Navajo, who call themselves Diné. Monument Valley, with its tall sandstone buttes, sits on the border of Utah and Arizona inside the Navajo Nation. Navajo weavers are famous for rugs woven on upright looms.
more: A large rug can take months to weave.

text: Utah is home to eight federally recognized tribes. They include the Ute, Paiute, Goshute, Northwestern Shoshone and Navajo peoples. They have their own governments, languages and ceremonies, and they are living in Utah today.
more: Many of the names on a Utah map began as words from these languages.

text: In July 1776, two Spanish friars, Domínguez and Escalante, left Santa Fe to find a route to California. They never reached it. They wandered through Utah, kept a daily diary, and came home after about 1,700 miles (2,700 km) in five months.
more: When winter closed in, they cast lots to decide whether to keep going. The lots said to go home.

text: On their way, the friars came down into a green valley with a big freshwater lake, now called Utah Lake. They wrote that the Ute people living there fished the lake and were friendly. Their diary gave the first written description of the valley.
more: Their map and diary were studied by mapmakers for years afterward.

text: In the winter of 1824 to 1825, a fur trapper tasted the water of a huge lake and spat it out. It was salty, so he told people he had found an arm of the ocean. The trapper is usually said to be Jim Bridger, and the lake was the Great Salt Lake.
more: Later trappers went all the way around it and found no outlet to the sea.

text: Each summer, trappers met at a rendezvous to trade beaver furs for supplies. Bear Lake, on the Utah and Idaho border, hosted the rendezvous in 1827 and 1828. Trappers and Native families camped there, traded, wrestled and raced horses.
more: A whole year of beaver furs might be traded away in a week.

text: In 1827, a trapper named Jedediah Smith and two companions crossed Utah's western desert on their way back from California. There was almost no water. Their horses gave out, and they walked, sometimes for days without a drink, until they reached the Great Salt Lake.
more: They were the first non-Native travelers known to cross that desert.

text: In the 1840s, the explorer John C. Frémont mapped much of this region. He found that its rivers, such as the Humboldt, never reach any ocean. They end in lakes or sink into the sand. He named the region the Great Basin.
more: Water that falls in the Great Basin never flows to the sea.

text: The Great Salt Lake is so salty that swimmers float like corks. In some parts it is several times saltier than the ocean. Few fish can live in it, but brine shrimp and brine flies thrive there by the billions.
more: Birds travel from far away to feed on them.

text: No river flows out of the Great Salt Lake. Rivers flow in, bringing a little salt each day, but water can leave only by rising into the air. The water evaporates and the salt stays behind. That is why the lake stays salty.
more: Rain and snow can make the lake rise, and dry years make it shrink.

text: A railroad causeway built of rock divides the lake in two. The south arm gets fresh river water. The north arm does not, so it is much saltier, and salt-loving microbes turn its water pink or red.
more: From the air the two arms are two different colors.

text: West of the lake lie the Bonneville Salt Flats, a flat white plain of hard salt that looks like a frozen lake. It is so smooth that racers have driven cars there to set land speed records for more than a hundred years.
more: The salt crust is only a few feet thick, and mud lies below it.

text: The Uinta Mountains are unusual: they run east to west, while most mountain ranges run north to south. Utah's tallest peak, Kings Peak, rises there to 13,534 feet (4,125 m).
more: From the top you can look across the whole high desert.

text: Utah is one of the driest states in the country. Most of it gets only about a foot of rain a year. But the mountains catch heavy winter snow, and the melting snow runs down in streams. Most of Utah's water begins as mountain snow.
more: That is why Utahns watch the snowpack all winter long.

text: On July 24, 1847, a company of pioneers rolled into the Salt Lake Valley. Their leader, Brigham Young, had been sick with a fever and came in a few days later. Looking out over the valley, he is remembered to have said, "This is the right place."
more: July 24 is still a state holiday in Utah. It is called Pioneer Day.

text: The pioneers were members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, looking for a place of their own. The first company was small: 148 people and 73 wagons. They left Winter Quarters, in what is now Nebraska, in April and traveled about 1,000 miles (1,600 km).
more: The trip took a little over three months.

text: To count the miles, William Clayton and Appleton Harmon made a roadometer. It was a wooden device on a wagon wheel, with gears that clicked once for each turn of the wheel. Clayton added up the clicks and wrote the distances in a guidebook.
more: Later pioneers used his guidebook, with the miles written down between landmarks.

text: When the pioneers arrived, the valley soil was dry and hard as brick. Within hours they dammed a stream, let the water spread over the ground to soften it, and planted potatoes. It was the settlers' first irrigation in the valley.
more: Their way of sharing water ditches spread to every town they founded.

text: From 1856 to 1860, about 3,000 pioneers crossed the plains pushing and pulling handcarts, two-wheeled wooden carts, because they could not afford wagons and oxen. Most companies arrived on time. Two arrived late in 1856 and were caught by early snow until rescuers reached them.
more: Rescue wagons were sent out from the valley with food and blankets.

text: In 1848, swarms of crickets began eating the settlers' first crops. People fought them with fire and shovels, but nothing worked. Then flocks of California gulls came and ate the crickets. A monument to the seagulls stands in Salt Lake City today.
more: The California gull is now Utah's state bird.

text: Salt Lake City was laid out in a grid with very wide streets, 132 feet (40 m) from edge to edge. Brigham Young wanted streets wide enough for a team of oxen and a wagon to turn around without backing up.
more: Those wide streets are why the city still feels so open today.

text: Addresses in Salt Lake City count out from the middle of town. The corner of Main Street and South Temple is the zero point. An address like 400 South 300 West means four blocks south and three blocks west of that corner.
more: Once you learn the system, you can find any address with no map.

text: The beehive became the symbol of Utah. Bees work together, build a home and store up for winter, and the settlers hoped to do the same. Utah is the Beehive State, its motto is Industry, and a beehive is on its seal.
more: Industry here means steady, hard work.

text: The Salt Lake Temple took 40 years to build, from 1853 to 1893. The granite blocks came from a canyon about 20 miles (32 km) away. At first, oxen pulled each block on a wagon, and one round trip could take four days.
more: Later a railroad carried the stone.

text: The settlers named their land Deseret, a word they took from their scripture that means honeybee. In 1850, Congress made it a territory instead and gave it the name Utah, after the Ute people.
more: The Territory of Utah was much bigger than the state is today.

text: Within a few years settlers built dozens of towns, some hundreds of miles from Salt Lake City: Provo, Ogden, Manti, Cedar City. In 1861 families were sent to the hot southwest corner to grow cotton. They built St. George, still known as Utah's Dixie.
more: Winters there are mild, and peaches and grapes grow well.

text: On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in northern Utah, two railroads met. A golden spike was set in a special tie, and telegraph wires carried the news across the country in one word: "Done." The two steam engines stood nose to nose.
more: A trip across the country that took months by wagon now took about a week.

text: Thousands of Chinese workers built the Central Pacific line through mountains and desert. On April 28, 1869, in Utah, crews laid 10 miles of track in a single day. It was a record that stood for many years.
more: It began as a bet between two railroad bosses.

text: In 1904, a railroad shortcut called the Lucin Cutoff opened across the Great Salt Lake. Trains rode on a wooden trestle almost 12 miles (19 km) long, built on piles driven into the lake bottom.
more: Trains still cross the lake there, on a rock causeway.

text: Bingham Canyon Mine, near Salt Lake City, is a copper mine dug as a giant open pit, started in 1906. It is about three-quarters of a mile (1.2 km) deep and 2.5 miles (4 km) wide. It is one of the largest holes ever dug by people.
more: Giant trucks with tires taller than a man haul the rock out.

text: Silver was found in the mountains near Park City in the 1860s, and a mining camp grew up. Miners dug tunnels deep into the mountain and sent silver ore out by wagon and rail. Today those same mountains hold ski runs.
more: Some old mine tunnels are still under the slopes.

text: In 1952, a prospector named Charlie Steen found a rich uranium deposit near Moab. Within a few years, hundreds of people rushed to southeastern Utah with Geiger counters to stake claims, and Moab became a boom town.
more: A Geiger counter clicks faster near uranium.

text: On January 4, 1896, President Grover Cleveland signed the paper that made Utah the 45th state. Bells rang, whistles blew, and a parade filled the streets of Salt Lake City.
more: Utah had asked to become a state many times before it got a yes.

text: On February 14, 1870, a young woman named Seraph Young cast her vote in Salt Lake City. She is usually counted as the first woman in the United States to vote under an equal-suffrage law.
more: Congress took the vote away in 1887, and Utah's new constitution gave it back in 1896.

text: Utah's state seal shows a beehive, sego lilies, an eagle and two flags, with the word Industry across the top. The sego lily is the state flower.
more: Pioneers dug up sego lily bulbs to eat when food ran short.

text: Utah has some unusual state symbols. The state bird is the California gull. The state animal is the Rocky Mountain elk. The state cooking pot is the Dutch oven. The state fossil is Allosaurus, a meat-eating dinosaur.
more: Very few states have chosen a cooking pot.

text: Martha Hughes Cannon, a doctor, ran for the Utah state senate in 1896 against her own husband. She won. She became the first woman state senator in the United States.
more: She also kept working as a physician.

text: In 1850, the Territory of Utah was much larger than the state is now. It stretched from California's mountains to the Rocky Mountains and included most of what is now Nevada. Over the next years Congress cut off pieces to make other territories and states.
more: Utah's borders took their final shape in 1868.

text: Utah has five national parks, called the Mighty Five: Zion, Bryce Canyon, Capitol Reef, Arches and Canyonlands. Each one shows a different side of the red-rock desert.
more: Together they cover more than a thousand square miles of canyons and cliffs.

text: Bryce Canyon is full of hoodoos, tall thin spires of orange and pink rock that stand in rows like a crowd. Bryce has more hoodoos than any other place on Earth.
more: Water freezes and thaws in the cracks of the rock more than 200 nights a year.

text: In Zion Canyon the Virgin River has carved a slot so narrow that hikers wade in the river itself. In the Narrows, the walls rise up to 1,000 feet (300 m), and in places the gap is only about 20 feet (6 m) wide.
more: After a storm upstream, the river can rise fast.

text: Delicate Arch stands alone on a bare rock ridge, 52 feet (16 m) tall, and it is on Utah's license plates. Arches National Park holds more than 2,000 natural stone arches, more than anywhere else in the world.
more: Wind, water and frost slowly wear the rock away.

text: In Dinosaur National Monument in northeastern Utah, a whole wall of rock is full of dinosaur bones, about 1,500 of them, left where they were found so visitors can see them. Earl Douglass found the first huge bones there in 1909.
more: You can touch the bones on the wall.

text: In 2002, Salt Lake City hosted the Winter Olympics. Utah's snow is famous because it falls light and dry, and ski towns call it the Greatest Snow on Earth. Some mountain resorts get more than 500 inches (12.7 m) of snow in a year.
more: Skiers come from all over the world to try it.
